utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Case Number IT-98-32-T, the Prosecutor versus Mitar Vasiljevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sorry for the late beginning, but there has been a small technical hitch that hasn't yet been cured, but we'll see how we are. Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, when we ended yesterday, the Court said we would start this morning by discussing two questions relative to the admission of this new piece of evidence. The first part of my remarks will be regarding whether -- regarding the inconsistencies that were brought up by Mr. Domazet on cross-examination and the relevance of this statement to those. And they are in two areas, Your Honour. The first one has to do with whether or not Mr. Vasiljevic was present when the people were moved from the Memic house to the Omeragic house. And I would refer the Court to the transcript, at the bottom of 79 to 80, and I will quote it here. Mr. Domazet asked: "My next question is: When you were talking about being taken from one house to the other house, the Omeragic house, you said today that Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic were there. My question, again, is: Can that be found in your statement to the investigator?"

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Will counsel slow down, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did you say that to the investigator of the Tribunal? And the witness answered in the affirmative, and Mr. Domazet sought to enter the statement to contravene that. Now, the Bosnian statement --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are we going to get all the issues that you want to address, or do you want to take each of them separately?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I prefer just to make my remarks, Your Honour, and then I'll leave it to the Court to decide --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: There's more than issue that he took with whether or not the witness had told the Prosecution's investigator these various matters. That was one.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And I will address that now, Your Honour, if that pleases you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The way I'm proposing to do it is to now refer to the part of the Bosnian statement which is germane to this and then move on to the second issue. In the Bosnian statement, quoting from that - the English translation of that -: "Once they had herded about 80 of us into that house, they set fire to something like gas at the front door, and big flames roared into the rooms where we were all crowded together." Then the last part of the statement, the person who made this statement identifies Mr. Vasiljevic as one of those persons. The second inconsistency which Mr. Domazet has introduced this statement -- or the witness's ICTY statement in relation to is whether or not Mr. Vasiljevic was present at the time that the witness and the other people were searched and their belongings were taken. And there are two portions in the transcript where Mr. Domazet does that. The first one is at page 80. And again, I am quoting: "Madam, if you didn't mention your neighbours, perhaps in this particular case it's not of essential importance. But it is very important if you are saying today that Milan Lukic and Mitar Vasiljevic took part in all these events; whereas earlier on, you said it was Milan Lukic and Sredoje Lukic. This is an important discrepancy. This is a very important discrepancy. So my question is: Could it not have been Sredoje Lukic who you omitted to mention, but instead of him, you have been mentioning Mitar Vasiljevic going from the plunder, looting, and the burning itself." And now I'm quoting from page 88 of yesterday's transcript. Mr. Domazet, question: "I have to ask you whether you remember that you stated in the statement to the investigator that Mitar had already left and it was after his departure that Sredoje Lukic arrived and you went on to give their description." And I believe there was a part of the transcript that was not decipherable as of yesterday when we were provided a copy of it. The answer to that question was: "Mitar Vasiljevic left after he had given the certificate to (redacted) (redacted), and during the plunder and mistreatment, they were all there again." Once again, Mr. Domazet introduced the ICTY statement for the purposes of showing that that was not in that statement. The Bosnian statement, again the person refers to "they": "They took all our money and gold." And once again at the end of that statement, the person who gave that statement identifies Mitar Vasiljevic as one of the perpetrators of that. Now, regarding whether we know -- whether I should be permitted to ask this witness whether she recognises this statement, I believe, Your Honour, yesterday -- well, I believe the standard is not whether I personally know whether this is, in fact, her statement but is whether I have a good-faith basis for showing the statement to her and asking her whether or not it is her statement. And I think there are three reasons, if we look at this statement, that we can tell that there is certainly a good-faith basis. One of the lines in the statement is: "I jumped out of the house with my 13-year-old son." For that very reason, Your Honour, we know that it must be either VG13 or VG18 in this case, and I would submit that that alone provides a good-faith basis for asking the question. But there is more. There's a quote in the statement that says: "I know for certain that only four of us managed to get out." At the end of the statement -- and, incidentally, the entire statement is written in the first-person, that is to say, from the point of view of the person making these claims. This person mentions the identities of three other people who she knows survived, and they are VG18, VG38, and Edhem Kurspahic. The fact that she mentions VG18 indicates that this statement was probably given by VG13, and in it she identified the three survivors aside from herself. This is also consistent with what we now know from both this witness and her son. At the time that this statement was given three months after the fire, this witness did not know that her son had survived the fire. And finally, Your Honour, if Your Honours were to review the statement of VG18, I believe that the Court would reasonably conclude that the statement from the Bosnians is more probably the statement of VG13. So on that basis, I think I do have a good-faith basis to show her the statement. Of course I am bound by her answer. If she says that she does not recognise it or it is not herself, I am bound by that answer. But I believe there's a good-faith basis for showing it to her.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You may proceed, Mr. Groome.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: I'd ask that Exhibit 59.1 be returned to the witness to look at.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Witness VG13, yesterday you had an opportunity to begin looking at the Document 59.1. Did you have an opportunity to finish reading it yesterday afternoon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG13 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Do you recognise or is this a statement that you gave? Do you recognise this statement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG13 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is it a statement that you gave to Bosnian authorities?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG13 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, at this time I would tender 59.1 and 59.2 into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Domazet, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I had objections yesterday, because this is not a statement given to any official body. It is part of a book by Naser Oric entitled "Srebrenica Witnesses/Accused." That is at least how I understand this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: It doesn't matter that it's not to an official body. The Prosecution would be entitled to produce any statement, oral even, one made to a newspaper, one made on a television programme. It doesn't have to be to an official body. You have drawn attention to the absence of any reference in her statement to the Prosecution of a number of matters. Now, the only reason you do so is to invite us to say that she is not telling the truth. That is a well-known process of cross-examination, but it does invite a response from the Prosecution that she may not have told the Prosecution about it but she's told other people about it. And this one has the virtue of being in September 1992. Now, have you got any objection on the basis that they are seeking to reinstate her credit as a witness because of your cross-examination that she had failed to tell the Prosecution's investigator about this?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, my question to the witness was whether she had made any statements to the MUP of Bosnia-Herzegovina. And I really would like to see that report, because she said, yes, the statement she actually made to the police of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because to my understanding this document may have been taken out of one such report, because it says here "we," not "I" but "we." "Among the four monsters, we recognised two." Milan Lukic is not mentioned at all, whom she did refer to extensively in her testimony, so that I really cannot recognise this to be a statement of this witness we have before you. Of course I shall be bound by your decision regarding this document and its admission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Domazet, that goes to the weight to be given to it. There is a very serious issue as to whether or not the reference in the penultimate paragraph to your client should be interpreted as having been the persons or one of the persons to whom she referred to throughout the whole of the statement. She has described him as one of the perpetrators, which could mean simply lighting the fire or being there shining torches on people when they are jumping out the window to enable somebody to shoot at them. That's a question of weight. It's not a question of admissibility. Is there anything more you want to say?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Despite your description of it as an exhibit, it is not yet an exhibit, but it will now become Exhibit P59.1. Is it necessary for it to be under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. It refers to the names of two protected witnesses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if you can make out who they are from it. But, anyway, we'll make it under seal. It will be Exhibit P59.1, and it shall be under seal. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And simultaneously 59.2, the English translation of that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's got a different number, has it?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Yes. 59.2 is the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that will be Exhibit P59.2, and it will also be under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Witness VG13, do you know a person by the name of Bula Kurspahic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG13 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Is that a man or a woman?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG13 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Did she die in the fire that night?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG13 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, and her two grandchildren and daughter-in-law.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And can you tell us, did she have children?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG13 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Without telling us their names, would you please tell us how many daughters and how many sons she had that you know of?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG13 [Resumed]
utterances.text: She had five daughters and two sons.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: And at the time that you made a statement to the ICTY investigator, which is now in evidence as D4, did you inform the investigator about Bula Kurspahic and her family being in Pionirska Street?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS VG13 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: Your Honour, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, madam, that's the end of your task here. We are very grateful to you for having come to give evidence and for the evidence that you have given. You are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Groome. Who is your next witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. GROOME
utterances.text: The next witness will be taken by Mr. Ossogo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo, I hope that this report will be tendered so that the doctor does not have to repeat anything in it. We've had the opportunity to read it, and you can add anything to it or explain it. You have to put his qualifications into evidence. But otherwise, we don't want you to take him through the report unless there is some particular matter you want him to add to it or to explain.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me, Mr. President, I didn't catch the interpretation on time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I was saying, Mr. Ossogo, I did not want you to take the witness through the report word for word. I want you to tender the report; and then if you want him to add anything or explain anything, you take him to those specific matters. We've had the opportunity to read the report; and subject to anything Mr. Domazet says about its admissibility, it can take the place of his evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. Quite. The examination of this witness this morning will be rather brief. We have not received any particular objection on the part of the Defence pursuant to Article 94 bis. When I disclosed this report to the Defence, they had no particular objection to it, so that fully fits into what you have just said. And the witness will be asked to explain only a few technical points, and we will undertake a very brief presentation of his curriculum vitae so we know the witness we have before us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, sir, would you stand up, please. Would you make the solemn declaration in the form of the document the court usher is handing to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Sit down, please, sir. Mr. Ossogo, we do have his curriculum vitae now filed. That's another way of shortening it. You should just tender it, I suggest.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite, Mr. President. May I begin, Mr. President?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. Clark.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I think you heard what the President has just said regarding the way in which the examination-in-chief should take place. So could you just indicate to us regarding your qualifications without, of course, repeating your curriculum vitae which the Judges have before them. Your name is John Clark, is it not?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You were born on the 5th of September, 1951?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You are a British citizen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: A graduate of the University of Aberdeen?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You specialised in forensic medicine, pathology, and you are a professor at Glasgow University in Scotland?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Not professor. Actually what we call a senior lecturer, which is equivalent to an assistant professor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: May I suggest, Mr. Ossogo, that you tender this document which was filed on Monday. Is there any objection to the curriculum vitae, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I don't want to intrude upon the Prosecution's numbering system. What's the next number which is available?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, it will be Document 61, Exhibit 61. JUDGE, HUNT: Thank you. The witness's curriculum vitae, Exhibit 61, P61. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have just told us that you are not actually a professor; but in French when you say "professor," it need not necessarily be a degree but it means that somebody teaches at the university. You're a member of a number of scientific associations, including the Royal College of Pathologists, and President of the Examining Board; is that right?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: What exactly does this scientific association engage in?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The Royal College of Pathologists is a United Kingdom organisation. It's the main professional association of pathologists throughout the country. It sets the standards and examinations for all pathologists, and I am in charge of the committee monitoring the forensic examinations.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Could you explain to us, very briefly, what does the work of a pathologist imply? The judges probably know this, but everyone is not aware of the scientific aspects of this profession.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, a pathologist, in general, is someone who looks and studies disease, and they look at diseased tissues, and they also carry out postmortem examinations on people to find out how they have died. A forensic pathologist has a particular expertise in looking at injuries and interpreting injuries; and, therefore, they have an expertise in examining the bodies of people who have died in suspicious and potentially criminal circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: So generally, you are working on human bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Are there any limits regarding your work, regarding the time that has elapsed since the person died, or can you work on any bodies regardless?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We can work on any body. But obviously, our findings are much easier to interpret the fresher the body is, if you like. And the longer the person has been dead, it become more difficult; not impossible, but much more difficult.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You are chief pathologist for the International Tribunal for the Former Yugoslavia based in Visoko. Your offices are in Visoko, aren't they?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. I have been chief pathologist in Bosnia and Croatia for the past three years.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Have you done any other project at the international level in your field of expertise?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes. As is indicated in my curriculum vitae, I have done a postmortem examination in Pakistan on the head of the chief of the army staff. I have also done work for the British Military Police, both in Kosovo and in Germany, and I have been involved in giving opinions in other international cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. Regarding your work, in connection with your current position, do you work outside your office, or do you always do your work in your own office when working on bodies?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I'm not sure if I follow that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Do you work on the sites where the bodies were found, or do you wait for them to be brought to you, to your offices?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, I work in the mortuary. The bodies are recovered by a separate team. They are brought to the mortuary, and that's where our work commences. I visit the site from time to time, and I'm well aware of the -- how the site teams work and the layout of the graves. But our work starts in the mortuary.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You spoke about teams. What is the makeup of your teams, technologically and scientifically speaking? Are they from the same country, the members of your team? Are they interdisciplinary, if I can put it that way? Do they come from different countries? Could you explain that, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: All of this is set out in his report, is it not, the team name, the countries they come from? Can't we just tender the report, and then go to anything you want to add to it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Quite, Mr. President. I am just focusing on certain points for credibility to assay -- to give the witness's credentials. This is a public hearing, so perhaps there are some details that are not generally known, because people don't have any access to procedure of this kind. So perhaps this throws more light on what the work entails, who the witness is and so on. But I will conclude Mr. John Clark's background, having said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: We were speaking, Mr. Clark, about the multidisciplinary composition of your teams, the teams helping you, I assume, in the work that you do at Visoko. Could you give us some specificities about that, give us a breakdown of that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, briefly, it is a very international team from many different countries, not all there at the same time. So there's a regular turnover. We have at any one time three pathologists, three forensic pathologists, and they are assisted by anthropologists, whose speciality is in examining bones. And we have a various series of crime officers: photographers, radiographer, secretaries, et cetera, as back-up staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You tabled a report to the Chamber and the Tribunal, dated the 10th of September of this year. And on the last page of that report, you have a series of names, and you say they are listed in the order in which they assisted you. Now, did you include all this in the synthesis you compiled?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I missed that question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: We can see it in the report. Please, Mr. Ossogo, let us proceed with what is important in this case. I know it's a public hearing. I know that a lot of people will not have access to the report, but we are not here to educate the public. We are here to hear a criminal trial, and we have a lot of work to do. Please, let's get on with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, Mr. President, your concern for moving on quickly, but I think it is important to know the overall report has been compiled from the individual postmortem reports completed by the team of pathologists, and so perhaps we could hear something about the way in which these postmortem reports were integrated Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. in his own final report, and this will indicate the responsibility of each of the pathologists.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: So were there postmortem reports incorporated into the overall report, Mr. John Clark? You yourself, sir, compiled the report according to standard procedure, and you encountered certain difficulties, you say. But we're not going to go back to those difficulties. However, there were limits concerning the bodies that you examined. You established that one of the principal difficulties you came across were that there was no more tissue, no tissue existed on the bodies, but you had to work with the bones alone. Could you elaborate, please? Could you explain what you mean? What was this particular difficulty that you encountered, the nature of it?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, that that was the main difficulty. These people had allegedly been in the ground for eight years. The bodies were reduced to skeletons, so all we had to look at was the bones. In our normal forensic practice, when we interpret injuries, it is very much done on looking at skin and soft tissues, looking for bruising and grazing and bleeding. And that can tell us, very clearly often, what specific thing caused the injuries and how old the injury was. If you remove all the skin and soft tissues and all we have left is the bones, then it becomes much more difficult, because if you break a bone just before you die, the actual damage to the bone will look exactly the same if you break the bone weeks after. So theoretically, since we just had the bones to look at, we couldn't be 100 per cent certain that any of the injuries that we found necessarily occurred in life, and they may well have occurred after death. So that was a sort of fundamental problem. We were also very much aware that there was a great potential for injuries to have occurred to the bodies after death. This could have occurred in various ways. It is alleged that these bodies floated down the river for 20 kilometres or so. There could have been damage during that period. They were recovered from the river and manhandled onto boats or whatever. Then they were buried. And over the years, with the bodies in the graves, the bones would become brittle, and the weight of the soil above could also cause fractures. So two things really: Because there was no soft tissue left, that made interpretation of injuries difficult, and there was a potential for injuries to have occurred after death. These were the main difficulties. There were other ones: interpretation of what exactly was a gunshot injury and what wasn't, and also in just working out what was the precise cause of death, because we find an injury to a bone. It's not an injury to a bone that kills you. It's the injury to the soft tissues roundabout in the internal organs which kills you. And if they are no longer there, we can only imply the cause of death rather than actually prove it. So these factors were very much borne in mind in our autopsies, and we worded our reports keeping that in mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Ossogo, every word of that is in the report. Rule 92 bis was introduced in order to prevent this very sort of thing happening. We have a report. We are not here to hear the doctor tell us what is in the report. Now, please tender it so that we can get on, and then once you've tendered it, you may take the doctor to expand anything you want him to expand. But please let us not have this way of introducing the evidence twice.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, we were going to tender the report after having asked those few questions, but we will proceed as you have just suggested. So we should like to tender the report under Number 60.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Any objection, Mr. Domazet?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. That will be Exhibit P60. And you may take it we've read it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. As the report has now been tendered and there has been no objections from the Defence --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. We need an original to become the exhibit, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, quite. Absolutely so. You already have copies, but the originals -- let me just see, take a moment. I apologise for that delay. The originals, I have just been told, have colours, and the last one that we sent you was the 10th of September. My assistant has just told me that the originals, in colour, will be available shortly later on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Okay. Let's proceed, and we'll look forward to those later.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Mr. Clark, you have just told us of the difficulties you encountered. Now, were there any insurmountable difficulties and, if so, which thesis did you adopt in compiling your report to the Tribunal if there were such difficulties? So how were you able to give us a final finding with respect to the cause of death, et cetera?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, I think I've explained the difficulties, and I have no more to add than what I said there.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Yes. I was talking about your thesis, the thesis you finally adopted on the basis of everything you saw and the difficulties you encountered. How were you able to summarise your findings as a pathologist? What rule did you follow in reaching the summary of the findings, in view of some of the insurmountable difficulties that you had?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, I took a common-sense attitude, because the difficulties I've just explained, the primary one being proving that the injuries occurred before or after death, if I was to say that all the injuries occurred after death, then we would have to allege that people had been shot deliberately after death, sometimes several times. And I took a common-sense attitude that that would seem to be most unlikely, and that was my general approach.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: So you were able to confirm death, ascertain death, prove death by gunshot or by the use of firearms?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, we found many bodies with gunshot injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: With respect to firearms, we find in your report - and it is on page 11 of that report - that you speak of two types of shots, two types of ammunition or shots which you found in the bodies, according to your report on page 11, different bullets. And on page 9, you also specify the type of gunshot wound entrance, bullet entrance hole, and the gunshot exit wound. Could you explain to us, looking at the figures found on page 9 and also what you say on page 4 -- we see an arrow. Could you tell us what that signifies? On figure 4 of page 9, the left-hand figure, figure 4 on page 9, there is an arrow on the dark surface, where you have the bullet entrance hole in the top of head. I'm referring to figure 4 of page 9. Could you explain what the arrow means?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, perhaps I could -- just to say that the vast majority of the gunshot injuries were what we interpret as high-velocity weapons, and we could interpret this for two reasons: the type -- the nature of the damage to the bone, where you get a huge amount of fragmentation and destruction, and also the fact that we found bullets and the remains of high-velocity bullets in a lot of the bodies. This skull here is a typical example of a high-velocity injury. You have the entrance hole just here, this circular hole in the top of the skull just to the left of the midline. It has caused a circular hole in the skull and it has also caused fractures, these long fractures running forwards and backwards and also to either side, and that's a very typical high-velocity entrance injury to the skull. The exit would have been at the bottom of the skull opposite and would have caused a great deal of damage. If you look at the second picture, this is a different case, but this shows almost the reverse, if you imagine the bullet coming from the bottom up out of the top, and this is the exit. And it's just to show the huge amount of destruction that a high-velocity weapon will cause in the skull. And that would be an immediately fatal -- fatal injury. There were two cases in which we found handgun bullets. These are much more low-velocity weapons, and they cause far less fracturing. They would probably just cause just the hole there without any fractures roundabout. They wouldn't cause all this damage. So in at least two cases, handguns were used, and possibly an additional two as well. But the vast majority, high-velocity weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: What you refer to as "high-velocity weapons," can you explain what you mean? What are high-velocity weapons? And if we look at page 11 of your report, page 11, you show bullets recovered from the bodies. "A" is a high-velocity rifle, and "B" is the example of a handgun used. Could you explain the difference?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The area of what we see, the bullets travel at much higher speeds in a high-velocity rifle, these automatic rifles, AK-47s, et cetera. The typical bullet is this one on the left, the sharp, pointed bullet. When it reaches the body, it not only causes a hole but causes huge pressure waves inside the body, which causes a huge amount of damage. And imagine that in the skull. It enters the skull and then causes huge pressure waves, which causes all the other fracturing. A handgun bullet from a pistol or a revolver is going at much less speed and really tends to just cause the physical damage as it goes through without any cavitation or surrounding effects.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: 130 individual bodies were examined. And in paragraph 5 of the conclusions made in your report, you say that 72 percent -- paragraph 5 of your report -- 72 percent say -- you say that people died from gunshot injuries. On the basis of your analysis and the examinations you did on the bodies, high-velocity bullets coming from special weapons, what was the percentage of high-velocity weapons with these 72 percent of people killed with gunshot injuries? What percentage were high-velocity weapons?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: We found only two with handguns. The figure is going to be about 70 percent of people. Roughly, 70 percent of people died from high-velocity gunshot injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. You also state, going back to page 9 of your report, that you were able to find 180 shots fired on the number of bodies. 54 percent were to the trunk, or 98; 27 percent were to the head, or 48; and that the arms and legs were -- 13 percent were to the arms and 6 percent to the legs. Could you explain to us, please, or give us your opinion as an expert witness on the fact that most of the shots were to the trunk, more than half, and the next in line were shots to the head, that is to say, 27 percent of those?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: The large number of shots to the trunk is not particularly surprising, because the trunk is the largest part of the body. So if you were to fire at somebody, you would have more chance than not of hitting the trunk. And these figures are very comparable to other cases that we have dealt with in Bosnia. The slightly surprising figure here is the lower level of shots to the legs. Now, in other sites, we've found a substantial number of shots to the legs. And bear in mind, the legs form a large part of the body surface as well. And this may or may not reflect how close the firer was to the victim. The closer the firer was, then the less chance, presumably, of striking the legs. It may reflect that. I don't know. But it's certainly an observation worth making, that there are less shots to the legs than in other cases that we have dealt with.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Can one say, therefore, that the lower number or percentage of shots to the legs is because the potential victims, if I can use the term, were in the hands of the killers and they weren't able to escape, they weren't able to run away?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's a possibility, or they were fired at close range. That would be my initial interpretation of that, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: You speak of cases where shots to the legs were more important, and there were more of those. Could you give us an idea of where you considered that to have been the case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, in some of the other grave sites we have dealt with in Bosnia, particularly the Srebrenica sites, in which the allegation was that people were shot from a little -- well, from some distance. Then there's a higher proportion of shots to the legs.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: In those cases, did you know who the victims were? Were they soldiers or civilians? Were you able to establish that?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: As far as we could establish, they weren't soldiers, so they were civilians, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: May we now move on to page 10, Doctor, please, page 10 of your report. Could you explain to us, please, the situation in which the shooters found themselves? That is to say -- what I mean by that is the position. In the cases, there were shots from behind to the head, 20, and the trunk, 37, from behind; the side, 13 shots to the head and 4 shots to the trunk; and shots from the front, 9 to the head, 24 to the trunk. How can you be certain of the position of the victims on the basis of the trajectory, the direction of the bullets, of where the bullets were lodged, or the configuration of the entrance holes or anything else?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: When somebody is shot in the head, we can usually find out the -- find the entrance hole when we stick the pieces together, and we can usually work out where the exit. So really, in all the case with shots to the head, we could tell where the bullet had entered. And the majority were either at the back of the head or the side of the head. And relatively few are at the front. Now, you could say, well, the people have been shot from behind or the side, but the head is very movable, so it would be possible, perhaps, for the firer to be in front of the person, and the victims' heads to the side. The bullet will go in the side, although you are actually facing the person. Similarly, with a shot to the top of the head, that does not necessarily mean that the firer was above the victim, because just by bending your head forward, you're going to expose the top of your head to the weapon. But generally, more shots were towards the back of the head, and the implication that more often than not, people were shot from behind. The trunk is a little more difficult. Again, as far as we could tell, more shots came from behind. It's a little more difficult to turn your trunk, so these are fairly genuine figures. But it's less easy when you're examining the bones in the trunk to determine a direction, and a lot of these cases, we couldn't tell. So that figure slightly dilutes the findings. But overall, more people were shot from behind than from any other direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Can we determine on the basis of those shots from behind, and with respect to the trunk, the entrance wounds or exit wounds, whether they were sporadic individual gunshots or a burst of gunshot -- a burst of gunfire? Were these shots from behind in a burst of gunfire or individual gunshots to the victims?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, a lot of them were individual shots. As I said in the table earlier, most people -- well, the majority of people had been shot just the once. So the majority of people who had been shot from behind probably was just a single shot. There were some people who had been shot up to six times, and that undoubtedly would be -- probably a burst of fire. But a mixture of both, but probably mainly one shot. I have stated these -- the next page, the top of the page, there are just examples of four cases, and they have all been shot just the once. First, one shot in the back of the head in the midline; secondly, to the side of the chest; another, one shot just once behind the right ear, and a young girl shot once in the back of the chest. So these are all individual shots, mainly from behind.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you now tell us whether it is possible -- we see it in your report, but in somewhat greater detail -- whether it is possible that these people died not as a result of gunshots, but as a result of shocks, falling into the water from a bridge? Was the percentage of such deaths significant or minimum, in your opinion?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: No, it was significant. In 28 percent of cases, we were not convinced that we had found a cause of death. There could be various reasons for that. One was that the injuries we found, say a gunshot injury, the pathologist did not consider that necessarily fatal. So if somebody is shot in the arm, that wouldn't necessarily kill you and you can survive that. And we found no other injuries, yet the person was dead, so they must have died for some other reason. Similarly, some people may have been shot through the abdomen, which is not going to damage the bones, so we would miss that. That was one group of people. Then there was a substantial group in which we actually found no injuries at all, no antemortem injuries, and one could only speculate that they may have died in other ways. The bodies were found in water, so there must be a possibility that they drowned. If they had been stabbed or cut-throat injuries, then we would not pick that up on a skeleton. If somebody had been strangled, that would be -- we wouldn't pick that up either. So there are other possible causes. Quite a number had been -- had what we call "blunt-force injuries." These are injuries nothing to do with gunshots but injuries caused by weapons, blows from weapons, or kicking, or even falling. And I have detailed seven cases in which there were very convincing blunt-force injuries. These would not necessarily be fatal, but they were certainly present.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you determine in this latter case whether it is possible to make a distinction between the blows that these people received, blunt-force blows, and the death that occurred following those?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Blunt-force injuries will not necessarily kill you, even a fractured skull or a blow from a weapon. It may render you unconscious but would not necessarily kill you. Potentially, if these people had been beaten and their bodies thrown into the river, then they would have drowned. That would be the probable cause of death, would be drowning. I can't prove drowning after eight years, so I couldn't give a cause of death. A gunshot injury to the head will necessarily kill you almost immediately. Blunt-force injuries will not necessarily do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Thank you. Doctor, let us go on to page 7 of your report. When those bodies were brought to you, there was clothing and personal effects found on those bodies. I understand, as you have said, that it is difficult to establish certain elements because of the state of the bodies when there was no soft tissue and the relationship between the bodies and certain effects found on them. But you did draw up a table on page 7 of the English version of your report from which it follows a certain number of elements that lead us to conclude that there was violence of some sort. We find figures of black, parcel-binding straps and other elements that you found. In your opinion, were these elements that assisted in exerting violence on the bodies that you examined subsequently?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, these were ten cases which I have detailed in which we found items in the bodies which we attributed to being ligatures or bindings, that these people had been -- either their wrists tied or the whole body tied together. The difficulty was that with these skeletonised remains, these ligatures were no longer actually in place around the wrists or necessarily around the body. But we certainly did find, when we unravelled them, loops, tied loops, which looked very much like the sort of loops you would put around somebody's wrists or somebody's waist. So that was our interpretation; these were ligatures and bindings.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: I should like to draw your attention, Doctor, to the horizontal columns, number 7 and 8, the two last ones that relate to women, F40 to 70 and F50 to 85 found in Slap 1. SP01 449B, there were two blankets that were found around the body secured by electrical wire around the chest and legs. Did you make any other findings regarding these blankets and the wire? Was this one body? Are you sure that it was only one body that was found?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, I think you have the numbers slightly mixed up, but it's the last two in the first section, if you like, 418B and 432B. These were both women. One had two blankets around her body, and these were tied by an electrical wire. The other one was just a blanket wrapped around the body without any bindings. These suggested to me that this is how these women had been -- ended up in the water, wrapped in blankets. Both of these were killed by gunshot injuries.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Were you able to establish any characteristics of these blankets, their colour; perhaps was anything written on them?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: As I recall, 418B, the blanket -- one was a sort of fawn-coloured -- light-brown-coloured blanket. The other one was a grey blanket with red designs on it. I don't think there was any writing on the blanket at all. They were examined more closely by scenes of crime officers. But as I recall, there was no identifying tags on the blankets.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Is it possible, even when there is no human tissue left on the bodies, to determine that there was violence exerted on the skeletons that you found?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: If there is damage to the skeleton, yes, that implies violence, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: Among these ten cases on your table, were you able to establish the nature of that violence?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Yes, we were able to find a cause of death in each one of these.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I have completed my questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Domazet.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Clark, I have a question for you, prompted by your answer to Mr. Ossogo's question, and that is: When asked whether the victims could have been military men, your answer was that the victims were not soldiers but civilians. My question is: On the basis of which elements were you able to ascertain that, in view of everything else that you have told us about, that is, regarding the time that has elapsed and the condition of the bodies or the skeletons when you were examining them? That is, in most cases there was no clothing found on them, which perhaps could have been one of the elements making possible your identification as to whether they were civilian or military?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: Well, to be correct, my response to that -- my answer about the military and civilian was not related to these -- these bodies. I was asked about another site, one of the Srebrenica sites, when commenting about distance. So I've actually made no comment about these victims being either military or civilian. My only observation was that we found, well, there were a mixture of males and females, young and old. And of the clothing that we found, none of it was military, and we found no weapons or bullets on any of these people. So although I can't exclude that this particular group of people, none of them were soldiers, there was certainly no positive evidence to point to them being military. But my comment, as I say, about civilian and military was related to another site entirely.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: I think I understand you now. But we are now talking about Site Slap, are we not, in this case?

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: I just explained that of this site, we found no positive evidence to suggest that these people were soldiers. As I've said, none of the clothing that we found was of military type. The victims were both male and female, children, adolescents, and older people.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes. But as far as I was able to understand, in a large number of cases, in view of the time that has elapsed, about nine years, there were very few such traces of clothing.

utterances.speaker: JOHN CLARK
utterances.text: That's not entirely true. We find -- found clothing or pieces of clothing in most bodies. And the clothing is carefully washed in the Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. mortuary and examined, and even though it's only a sleeve of a shirt or something, we can usually tell if that's military or not. And there was no evidence of that in any of these cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I have no additional questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Mr. Ossogo?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSSOGO
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, Doctor, for coming along to explain it all to us. We are very grateful to you for coming, and you are now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Domazet, I understand you have a personal matter which you have to attend to, which will mean you won't be here tomorrow or Friday. I also understand that the witnesses who were nominated for tomorrow will be called now on Monday, and then we'll finally end up the Prosecution case on Tuesday with Dr. de Grave. Do you see any particular problem? I'm thinking of the time that you're going to have available after the close of the Prosecution case before your case opens, but I'm anxious that there should be no prolongation of the evidence beyond Tuesday so that you do have the end of that week and the next week to be ready.

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. If we complete the Prosecution case on Monday and Tuesday - and I hope we will be able to do that - it is my understanding that we would resume on Monday, the 22nd of October.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's right. And then the following week, unfortunately we will not be able to sit. Hopefully, if you can get us your list of witnesses and their summaries and everything by the Friday beforehand, then we will have the Pre-Defence Conference on the Monday and you can open your case on the Tuesday. If you like, we'll leave making any orders about it and see how we go on Monday and Tuesday. But my purpose in raising it at this stage is to obtain from you, which I have obtained from you, your hope that we will conclude all of the Prosecution evidence by Tuesday. And if that's so, it seems to me that's the way we'll proceed, with those documents you have to file by the Friday before the 22nd, the Pre-Defence Conference on the Monday, and you open on the Tuesday, but with the understanding that we will not be sitting the following week. Is there anything else that we can deal with at this stage?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as I have been able to see, according to the schedule, Mr. Yves Roy has been proposed, the investigator. Perhaps his examination could take place today instead of leaving it for Tuesday; if possible, of course. I'm quite prepared for other witnesses too today, but apparently these two witnesses are still not ready to testify. That is my understanding of what I was told by the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: They are the ones who were subpoenaed to attend, do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. DOMAZET
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I think Mr. Groome told us they were coming in yesterday, last night or something. And that's obviously where he is now. But what about the investigator?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: Your Honour, may we take the adjournment to try to figure that out?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, by all means. Well, as I understand it, Mr. Roy is going to give very short evidence, and we can assemble at any time today when he's available. If any of these subpoenaed witnesses are ready during the day, we'll hear them as well. It's best to get as much of this done as possible so there can be no likelihood of the evidence spilling beyond Dr. de Grave on Tuesday. We'll adjourn, and we won't resume until we hear from you. But we would like to hear from you as to the progress of your inquiries, Ms. Bauer. That's all. Will that be all right?

utterances.speaker: MS. BAUER
utterances.text: We'll do so as soon as we know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. All right. We'll adjourn now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: at 10.52 a.m. to be reconvened on Monday, the 8th day of October, 2001, at 9.30 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25
